I analysed a 600 × 600 m area around Chalmers (EPSG:3006 bounds 319200, 6397700, 319800, 6398300). I used a 2 m ground-only DEM built from 745,574 LiDAR points. I rendered the terrain mesh above, but it shows only elevation. The slope values below have no spatial breakdown, so I can't say where the steep parts are.

**Elevation (DEM)**
- The range is 41.4–86.9 m, about 45 m of relief.
- The mean is 61.4 m and the median is 62.2 m.
- The 5th–95th percentile range is 46.5–75.0 m.

**Slope**

The tool returns slope in radians. The aspect range of ±π suggests the same unit, so I converted to degrees.

| Statistic | Radians | Degrees |
|---|---|---|
| Median | 0.074 | about 4.2° |
| Mean | 0.154 | about 8.8° |
| 95th percentile | 0.553 | about 31.7° |
| Max | 1.291 | about 74° |

**Interpretation**
- Most of the area is gentle or flat. Half of the cells are under about 4°, which is typical of built-up campus ground.
- The distribution is skewed. The mean is about twice the median, and a minority of cells are steep, with the top 5% above about 32°.
- The steepest cells (up to about 74°) are probably rock outcrops, embankments, cuttings and retaining walls. They may also be artefacts where ground points are sparse under buildings and the DEM is interpolated. I can't confirm either from these statistics.
- The aspect raster covers the full ±π range, so there is no single dominant slope direction in the summary.

I can re-run at a finer cell size, such as 1 m. I can also export the slope raster as a TIF or CSV so you can map it in GIS.

I downloaded the point cloud for central Gothenburg. The tool refused a single 5 × 5 km request (25 km²) because its limit is 10 km² per download. So I split the area into four 2.5 km tiles, and all four downloaded and are stored.

The area is centred on Göteborgs central station (E 319676, N 6400380 in EPSG:3006). It spans x 317176–322176 and y 6397880–6402880.

| Tile | Object ref | Points |
|---|---|---|
| SW | `obj_490c6002` | 12,608,738 |
| SE | `obj_08694987` | 13,992,893 |
| NW | `obj_ec7c0775` | 10,798,720 |
| NE | `obj_104dfa4f` | 10,370,964 |
| **Total** | | **≈47.8 million** |

- **Classes:** each tile has unclassified (1), ground (2), noise (7), water (9), bridge (17) and class 18 points. The ground and unclassified counts are roughly equal in each tile. Class 18 is the smallest group.
- **Outliers:** the elevation ranges include some clear noise, such as −334 m in the NE tile and +568 m in the SE tile. The median elevation is about 7–29 m. I didn't filter these, so you'd want `remove_outliers=true` or a classification filter before building terrain.
- **Separate tiles:** they're four separate objects, not one merged cloud.

I can build terrain meshes or rasters per tile, filter to ground or buildings only, or export the tiles. At roughly 10–14 million points each, exporting or rendering will be heavy, so I'd suggest working per tile or on a filtered subset.

The terrain around Chalmers (a 600 × 600 m area centred on 319500, 6398000 in EPSG:3006) is mostly gentle, with some steep sections. The render shows the terrain mesh only. It has no slope field on it, so I can't say where the steep parts are.

**Elevation** (412k ground points, 2 m DEM)
- Elevation runs from 41.3 m to 87.1 m, a relief of about 46 m.
- The mean is 61.5 m and the median is 61.9 m.
- The 5th to 95th percentile range is 46.5 to 75.0 m.

**Slope** (from the 2 m DEM)

The slope raster appears to be in radians, since the aspect values span ±π. I converted to degrees on that assumption.

| Statistic | Radians | Degrees |
|---|---|---|
| Median | 0.074 | about 4.2° |
| Mean | 0.154 | about 8.8° |
| 5th percentile | 0.007 | about 0.4° |
| 95th percentile | 0.553 | about 31.7° |
| Max | 1.291 | about 74° |

- **Mostly gentle:** the median slope is about 4°, so at least half the area is nearly flat.
- **Skewed by steep terrain:** the mean is about twice the median. The top 5% of cells are steeper than about 32°, and the maximum is about 74°. Those steep cells are probably embankments, cuts and rock outcrops. That is my interpretation, because the statistics don't give locations.
- **Aspect:** the aspect values cover the full ±π range, with a median near 0 rad. They are summary statistics only, so they give no dominant slope direction I can name.

The slope and aspect rasters are stored as `obj_27dd549c` (slope) and `obj_7d4e7e73` (aspect). I can export them as GeoTIFF or CSV. I can also repeat the analysis on a smaller area, such as the Chalmers campus core, or on a finer 1 m grid.

**Terrain slope around Chalmers**

The area is a 600 × 600 m box centred on Chalmers (EPSG:3006: 319200–319800 E, 6397700–6398300 N). I built a 2 m DEM from 412,446 ground-classified lidar points and computed slope from it.

**Elevation**
- The range is 41.3 to 87.1 m, so the relief is about 46 m.
- The mean is 61.5 m and the median is 61.9 m.
- The 5th to 95th percentile range is 46.5 to 75.0 m.

**Slope**

The tool returned slope in radians. I converted to degrees, assuming the values are radians, which matches the aspect range of ±π.

| Statistic | Radians | Degrees |
|---|---|---|
| Median | 0.074 | about 4.2° |
| Mean | 0.154 | about 8.8° |
| 5th percentile | 0.007 | about 0.4° |
| 95th percentile | 0.553 | about 31.7° |
| Max | 1.291 | about 74° |

- **Mostly gentle:** half of the cells are under about 4°, so the campus core is relatively flat.
- **Steep tail:** the mean is about twice the median, and the top 5% of cells exceed about 32°. That points to a few steep slopes, probably rock outcrops or embankments. The tool gives no locations, so I can't say where they are.
- **Aspect:** it covers the full −π to π range with a mean near 0 and a median of −0.20 rad. That means no single dominant slope direction in these summary figures.
- **Possible artifacts:** the very steepest cells (up to 74°) may come from sharp terrain edges or from gaps where buildings were removed from the ground points. I haven't checked this.

A single 5 × 5 km request (25 km²) was refused because the download limit is 10 km². The geocoder also matched only Göteborg Central Station and returned a box of about 650 × 1,090 m. I used its center (319676, 6400379, EPSG:3006) and built a 5 × 5 km box around it: x 317176–322176, y 6397880–6402880. I then split that into five 1 × 5 km west-to-east strips.

| Strip | x range | Object | Points |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (west) | 317176–318176 | `obj_008a1ead` | 10.61 M |
| 2 | 318176–319176 | `obj_730f2e56` | 8.30 M |
| 3 (center) | 319176–320176 | `obj_c3ec0706` | 9.02 M |
| 4 | 320176–321176 | `obj_e68dc641` | 8.83 M |
| 5 (east) | 321176–322176 | `obj_945894e4` | 11.01 M |

- **Classes:** Each strip is about 45–50% ground (class 2) and 40–50% unclassified (class 1). The rest is small amounts of noise (7, 18), water (9) and bridge (17) points.
- **Water points:** Strips 1 and 2 have the most, with 477k and 204k.
- **Elevation outliers:** The data includes noise. Elevations run from about −334 m to +568 m, even though the 5th–95th percentile range is only about 0–73 m. I'd filter out classes 7 and 18, or use `remove_outliers`, before building terrain.
- **Rendering:** I didn't render the full cloud because 47.8 M points is too many to draw usefully.

For terrain or building models, I'd run it per strip, for example `classification_filter` for ground, then `build_terrain_raster` and a surface mesh. A smaller area, such as 3 km across, would let you work on it as one object. Do you want me to do either?
